messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Midwife
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed, Male Presence: Being alone with men, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied, Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Priya is a sixty-six-year-old South Asian woman who has worked as a midwife for nearly four decades, a vocation she has always described as a calling. She is married, the mother of adult children, and by most outward measures a figure of quiet authority in the labor and delivery ward where she has spent the better part of her professional life. She presented for assessment with a PCL-5 score of 74, referred by her primary care physician after she disclosed, haltingly and for the first time, that something had happened to her during a military medical deployment many years ago — something she had spent the intervening decades trying to outrun.

During that deployment, Priya had been assigned to a forward medical unit. One night, a senior officer entered the supply room where she was working alone. What followed was a sustained episode of sexual coercion and threatened violence by a man in uniform whose rank made her silence feel like the only survivable option. She remembered the fluorescent light above flickering. She remembered being watched — his eyes tracking her every movement as though cataloguing her. She remembered the particular way a man's presence in a confined space could fill it entirely, leaving no air. These are not memories she has words for easily; they are, instead, the architecture of her present fear.

In the years after the deployment, Priya noticed that certain moments would pull her back without warning. A male colleague stepping into the medication room while she was alone, a security guard in uniform pausing near the nurses' station, the sensation of being observed by a supervisor during a procedure — each of these would snap something taut inside her. What she felt was not merely discomfort. Her body moved immediately into a state of high alert: scanning the room, tracking exits, watching hands and posture for the first sign of threat. She became superalert in ways she could not fully explain to herself, unable to settle even in the staff break room when she knew, rationally, that she was safe. Sudden movements by male colleagues — a hand reaching past her, a door swinging open — would send a bolt of alarm through her chest before she had time to think. The triggers she encountered most reliably were not abstract; they were woven into the daily fabric of a busy hospital ward, and each one reliably ignited the same state of vigilant, unrelenting threat.

Because that state was so unbearable, Priya had, over the years, built her life around managing it. She had become expert at never being alone with a man — scheduling her breaks carefully, positioning herself near other nurses, finding reasons to step out when a male physician lingered. She began working longer and longer hours, filling every quiet moment with tasks, because stillness allowed the vigilance to turn inward and become unbearable. Hypervigilance toward people in general had become a constant low-level occupation: she read body language compulsively, assessed every new face on the ward, and kept herself oriented toward the room's exits as a matter of habit. These strategies had, in their way, worked — they had kept her functioning, kept her present at bedsides, kept her marriage intact in a surface sense. But they had also narrowed her world considerably. She had declined a promotion to ward manager because the role would have required one-on-one meetings with male administrators in closed offices. She had stopped attending the monthly clinical reviews. Her husband had noticed her restlessness at home, her inability to sit quietly in the evenings, though she had never told him why.

What Priya had not anticipated was the way her strategies fed the very sensitivity she was trying to manage. By never being alone with men, she had ensured that male presence remained charged with danger; by scanning every room for threat, she found it everywhere. The constant vigilance that was meant to protect her kept her nervous system primed, so that each new trigger — a uniform, a gaze, a man at the edge of her peripheral vision — landed with full force. The loop had been tightening for years without her naming it.

What finally brought her in was a moment on the ward when a young male student midwife, well-meaning and oblivious, touched her shoulder briefly to get her attention. She had flinched so visibly that a colleague asked if she was all right. Standing in the corridor afterward, she had thought: I cannot keep living like this. What she most fears is that the damage is permanent. What she most hopes is that someone will tell her it is not.
